title: Hands in the Earth — Growing a Mediterranean Herb Garden
excerpt: Rosemary, basil, oregano, lavender — the herbs of the Mediterranean are medicine, flavor, and therapy in one. How to grow them anywhere, and why your hands in the soil matters more than you think.
body:
Before I am a painter, I am a gardener. Every morning in Palermo, before the light gets too strong, I am outside with my hands in the dirt. Watering the basilico. Pinching back the rosmarino. Checking whether the lavanda has started to bloom.

This ritual is not just about growing food. It is about growing calm.

Research published in the Journal of Health Psychology found that gardening reduces cortisol more effectively than other leisure activities, including reading. The act of touching soil exposes you to Mycobacterium vaccae, a natural bacterium that triggers serotonin production in the brain. Thirty minutes in the garden, a few times a week, measurably reduces anxiety and depression.

The Mediterranean herbs are especially forgiving for beginners. They evolved in rocky, dry, sun-baked conditions — they do not need much water, rich soil, or attention. What they need is light and drainage.

Here is how to start, even on a balcony:

Rosmarino (Rosemary) — The most resilient herb I know. Plant it in a terracotta pot with sandy soil and forget about it. Water only when the soil is completely dry. It will give you fragrance, flavor, and small blue flowers that the bees love.

Basilico (Basil) — The soul of Sicilian cooking. Needs more water than rosemary but still prefers sun. Pinch the flower buds as they appear — this keeps the leaves producing. A pot of basil on a sunny windowsill will transform your kitchen.

Origano (Oregano) — Wild oregano grows everywhere in Sicily, between rocks and along stone walls. In a pot, give it full sun and let it dry between waterings. Dry the sprigs by hanging them upside down — dried Sicilian oregano is more potent than fresh.

Lavanda (Lavender) — Not just beautiful. Lavender essential oils have been clinically shown to reduce anxiety. I keep several pots near my studio door. The scent meets me every time I step outside.

Menta (Mint) — Grows aggressively, so keep it in its own pot or it will take over. Perfect for tea, for granita, for pressing into a glass of cold water on a hot afternoon.

The connection between gardening and well-being is not metaphorical. When you plant a seed and tend it, you are practicing patience, presence, and care — the same qualities that sustain a painting, a meal, or a life. The garden teaches you that growth is slow, seasonal, and worth the wait.
author: Milly Farfalla
